1.title: A Letter Without Thanksgiving
1.context: Paul’s letters usually open with thanksgiving and prayer for the readers. Galatians goes straight to the sender’s credentials, because the teachers troubling the churches had made Paul’s authority itself the issue.
1.question: When something you carry has to be defended, what do you reach for first: your record, your relationships, or the truth of the thing itself?

1.title: Grace and Peace, and a Rescue
1.context: The greeting packs the letter’s whole gospel into five verses: Christ gave himself to rescue, not merely to advise. The present evil age is Paul’s name for the world his readers were being pulled back into.
1.question: Paul describes salvation as a rescue from the present age. What would it mean for you to be rescued from yours?

1.title: Deserting the One Who Called You
1.context: Deserting is a soldier’s word for leaving a post. Paul frames the Galatians’ turn not as growth or open-mindedness but as defection from the God who called them.
1.question: Is there a place where you have quietly drifted from what you first believed? What pulled you?

1.title: Even an Angel
1.context: The curse is stated twice, and Paul notes he had given the Galatians the same test in person. No messenger, however impressive, outranks the message once delivered.
1.question: What would you refuse to believe even if it came from the most impressive voice you know?

1.title: Seeking the Approval of Men
1.context: The teachers’ charge was that Paul’s gospel was tailored to please its hearers. His answer turns on the word still: the man he used to be had built a career on men’s approval.
1.question: Whose approval most tempts you to edit what you believe?

2.title: Not Devised by Man
2.context: Revelation, not instruction, is Paul’s claim for his gospel’s origin. The rest of the chapter is offered as evidence, in the form of dates and places his readers could check.
2.question: What conviction of yours would survive being told you had invented it?

2.title: Advancing Beyond Many
2.context: Paul does not soften his past: the church he now builds is the church he tried to destroy. His zeal for the traditions of his fathers was the very engine of the persecution.
2.question: What were you once most zealous about that you now see differently?

2.title: Pleased to Reveal His Son
2.context: Set apart from his mother’s womb echoes the callings of Jeremiah and of the Servant in Isaiah. Paul reads his own call as set in motion long before Damascus, and Arabia, not Jerusalem, as its first classroom.
2.question: Where might God have been at work in your life long before you noticed?

2.title: Fifteen Days, Under Oath
2.context: Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name. The visit’s brevity is the argument: three years of independence and a fortnight’s stay cannot produce a gospel learned from the apostles.
2.question: What detail of your story would you swear to, because everything else hangs on it?

2.title: Unknown by Sight in Judea
2.context: Acts shows Paul in Jerusalem more often than this letter counts, and the two accounts were never harmonized by their authors. Paul’s point stands on his own ledger: the Judean churches knew his preaching only by report, and glorified God for it.
2.question: Who has been affected by your story without ever having met you?

3.title: Fourteen Years Later
3.context: Paul does not say whether this visit is the famine trip of Acts 11 or the council of Acts 15, and readers have argued both for centuries. His concern is not the date but the verdict Jerusalem gave his gospel.
3.question: When have you laid your work before people whose judgment you respected, afraid it might all be in vain?

3.title: Not Even Titus
3.context: Titus, a Greek believer traveling with Paul, became the test case: if circumcision were required of Gentiles, it would be required of him, in Jerusalem, in front of the leaders. It was not.
3.question: Who is being quietly tested, in your world, to see whether they really belong?

3.title: They Added Nothing to Me
3.context: Entrusted is a steward’s word: the gospel was placed in Paul’s hands by God, and the pillars’ audit found it whole. Peter’s field and Paul’s field are presented as one commission in two directions.
3.question: What has been entrusted to you that you must neither shrink nor pad?

3.title: The Right Hand of Fellowship
3.context: The right hand was a pledge of partnership. The single request attached, remembering the poor, matches the famine relief that runs through Acts and Paul’s later collection for Jerusalem.
3.question: What partnership in your life began with agreement on the main thing and one simple shared duty?

3.title: Opposed Him to His Face
3.context: Paul never records Peter’s answer at Antioch, and Acts never mentions the confrontation at all. The letter lets the rebuke stand as its own evidence that no carrier of the gospel, however senior, is above it.
3.question: When have you seen a good person compromise at a table or a moment of pressure? What did it cost?

4.title: Not Justified by Works of the Law
4.context: Justified is courtroom language: declared in the right. This sentence, aimed first at fellow Jews, becomes the doctrinal center of the whole letter.
4.question: What are you still trying to be declared in the right about, and before whom?

4.title: Crucified with Christ
4.context: Paul answers the charge that grace licenses sin by pointing at his own death and new life. If righteousness came through the law, he reasons, the cross was wasted effort, and he will not set grace aside to say so.
4.question: What part of your old life do you most need to reckon as crucified rather than merely improved?

4.title: Who Has Bewitched You?
4.context: Paul appeals to the Galatians’ own experience of the Spirit, received by hearing with faith before any law-keeping was asked of them. The argument is a memory test.
4.question: What did you receive by simply hearing and believing, before you could earn anything?

4.title: Abraham Believed God
4.context: The quoted line is Genesis 15:6, spoken of Abraham years before his circumcision in Genesis 17. Paul builds the order into an argument: faith was credited as righteousness first.
4.question: What does it change for you that Abraham’s standing with God rested on believing a promise?

4.title: Becoming a Curse for Us
4.context: Paul strings together quotations from Deuteronomy, Habakkuk, and Leviticus to set the two roads side by side. The tree of Deuteronomy’s curse becomes, in his reading, the cross where the curse was absorbed.
4.question: Where have you seen someone take a cost that by rights belonged to someone else?

5.title: Four Hundred and Thirty Years Later
5.context: The 430 years echoes the span Exodus gives for Israel’s time in Egypt. Paul’s lawyerly point: a ratified covenant is not amended by a document that arrives centuries later.
5.question: What promise in your life predates the complications that now seem to govern it?

5.title: Why Then Was the Law Given?
5.context: Added because of transgressions: the law’s role was real but temporary and indirect, delivered, Paul says, through angels by a mediator, where the promise came from God himself.
5.question: What in your life was a genuine help for one season that you are tempted to make permanent?

5.title: Our Guardian
5.context: The guardian, the paidagogos, was a household slave who escorted a child to school and supervised his conduct. Paul treats the office as honorable, necessary, and finished when faith comes.
5.question: What discipline guarded you well in an earlier season that you no longer live under?

5.title: All One in Christ Jesus
5.context: The three pairs, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, name the ancient world’s deepest divisions. Paul’s sentence has been read at baptisms ever since, where the divisions are left at the water.
5.question: Which of your labels matters least where your standing with God is concerned?

5.title: Abba, Father
5.context: Adoption language was Roman law at its most generous: an adopted son held full heir’s rights. The Spirit’s cry uses Jesus’ own Aramaic word for father, heard earlier in Mark’s telling of Gethsemane.
5.question: What would change if you addressed God with a child’s word rather than a subject’s?

6.title: Turning Back
6.context: Known by God reverses the direction of the relationship mid-sentence. The days and months and years are the calendar of observance the Galatians were adopting, which Paul reads as a return to their pagan past in new dress.
6.question: What spiritual habit of yours has quietly become a chain?

6.title: You Would Have Torn Out Your Eyes
6.context: Paul first reached Galatia because of an illness, a detail Acts does not mention. The eyes remark has long suggested the affliction involved his sight, but the letter itself never names it.
6.question: Who received you kindly at your weakest, and how do you keep from becoming their enemy across distance or time?

6.title: Zealous, But Not in a Good Way
6.context: The image turns maternal: Paul in labor pains, again, until Christ is formed in them. Formation, not mere information, is his stated goal for the churches he founded.
6.question: Whose formation are you laboring over, and what makes it feel like starting again?

6.title: Two Covenants
6.context: Paul reads the Hagar and Sarah story as an illustration of two covenants, slavery under Sinai and freedom in the promise. The Isaiah quotation celebrates the barren woman whose children outnumber the married wife’s.
6.question: In Abraham’s household, which child’s story resembles yours: born by arrangement, or born by promise?

6.title: Children of the Free Woman
6.context: The expulsion saying is Sarah’s demand in Genesis 21, which God told Abraham to honor. Paul applies it to the teachers’ program: the slave woman’s line does not share the inheritance.
6.question: What old arrangement needs to be sent away so the promise in your life can hold the whole house?

7.title: Christ Will Be of No Value
7.context: Fallen away from grace is aimed at the law-relying, not the struggling: Paul’s catastrophe is a changed system of justification, not a bad week. Faith expressing itself through love is his one-line summary of what counts.
7.question: What yoke have you been set free from that still tries to re-enlist you?

7.title: A Little Leaven
7.context: The wish in verse 12 is aimed at the circumcision party’s own logic, and it shocked ancient readers as it does modern ones. Paul leaves it unrepeated and unsoftened, and moves on to freedom’s real dangers.
7.question: What small influence in your life is working through the whole batch, for good or ill?

7.title: Serve One Another in Love
7.context: The single decree is Leviticus 19:18, the same love command Jesus and Paul both make the law’s summary. Biting and devouring pictures a congregation consuming itself, the flesh’s favorite use of freedom.
7.question: How could you use one freedom you enjoy this week to serve somebody else’s interest?

7.title: Walk by the Spirit
7.context: The flesh and the Spirit are presented as opposing occupants of one life, so that inner conflict is a mark of the Spirit’s presence rather than his absence.
7.question: Where do you most feel the opposition Paul describes, and what does walking, rather than winning outright, look like there?

7.title: The Fruit of the Spirit
7.context: Works are manufactured; fruit is grown. Paul’s list of nine has been counted as one fruit with nine flavors, since the word fruit is singular and love stands first.
7.question: Which of the nine do you most need grown in you this season, and what conditions grow it?

8.title: Carry One Another’s Burdens
8.context: Burdens and load are different Greek words in the text: the crushing weight is carried together, the soldier’s pack is carried alone. Paul sets the two side by side without explaining them away.
8.question: Whose crushing burden could you help carry this week, and which pack is yours alone to carry?

8.title: Whatever a Man Sows
8.context: Sowing and reaping is the letter’s last word on the flesh and the Spirit: the two fields of chapter 5 become two harvests. Due time sets the pace; harvests do not run on the sower’s schedule.
8.question: What are you sowing now, almost invisibly, that you will one day be glad or sorry to reap?

8.title: Large Letters, My Own Hand
8.context: Paul commonly dictated his letters and signed the close himself; here the large letters may serve as emphasis, eyesight, or both. What matters to his argument is the shift into his own hand for the motives he now names.
8.question: What would you write in large letters, in your own hand, if a message had to be unmistakably yours?

8.title: A New Creation
8.context: The world crucified to Paul and Paul to the world: the cross ends the old order’s claims in both directions. The Israel of God in the blessing has been read both as the church and as believing Israel; Paul leaves the name standing without defining it further.
8.question: What boast have you retired, and what has taken its place?

8.title: The Marks of Jesus
8.context: Marks carried the sense of a slave’s brand or a soldier’s scars: ownership written on a body. The letter that opened without thanksgiving closes with the warmest of its benedictions, grace with your spirit, brothers.
8.question: What have you borne, in body or in life, that has become a credential you would not trade?
